segments.translit: sahajamadamudito hi bhūsukupādas tam evārthaṃ prakaṭayati—
segments.translation: [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku}, delighted by the intoxication of the [innate]{sahaja}, makes that very meaning manifest:
segments.note: Munidatta introduces the song by saying that [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku}, delighted by the intoxication of the [innate]{sahaja}, makes 'that very meaning' manifest (cp.43.m1). He does not say which meaning he has in mind.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) reads lhan cig skyes pa'i bde bas tshim pa, 'satisfied by the bliss of the innate', for sahajamadamudita, 'delighted by the intoxication of the innate', and de kho na nyid kyi don, 'the meaning of reality', for tam evārtham, 'that very meaning'. It also translates the poet's name ('du shes gsum pa'i zhabs). I translate the Sanskrit.

In Munidatta's opening (cp.43.m1), tam evārtham, 'that very meaning', has nothing to point back to inside this song's comment. He may mean the truth his comments keep returning to, or something said earlier. I keep it literal rather than supply 'reality' from the Tibetan.

segments.translit:
sahaja ityādi| gurucaraṇareṇuprasaṅgena pavipadmasaṃyogasukhākārabījaṃ gṛhītvā trailokyaṃ vyāpya yogīndrasya sahajacitta[ṃ] sphuritaṃ(taḥ)| etasya khasamopamasukhasvabhāvena trailokye na ko vidvān mukto veti|
tathā ca dvikalpe—
vyāpyavyāpakarūpeṇa sukhena vyāpitaṃ jagat|
padasyottarapadena dhruvapadaṃ boddhavyaṃ|
segments.translation:
'The [innate]{sahaja}…' and so on. Through contact with the dust of the [guru]{guru}'s feet, having taken the [seed]{seed} that has the form of the [bliss]{sukha} of the union of [vajra]{vajra} and [lotus]{lotus}, the [innate]{sahaja} [mind]{citta} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} has [radiated]{sphurana}, pervading the [three worlds]{trailokya}. Through its [sky-like]{khasama} [nature]{svabhava} of bliss, no one in the three worlds is [bound]{bandhana} or freed.
And so in the [Dvikalpa]{tx-hevajra}:
'The [world]{jagat} is pervaded by bliss in the form of [pervaded and pervader]{vyapya-vyapaka}.'
The [refrain]{dhruvapada} is to be understood by the latter part of the [verse]{pada}.
segments.note: Munidatta's paraphrase puts the [innate]{sahaja} [mind]{citta} of the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} where the song has the great tree: through the dust of the [guru]{guru}'s feet it has taken the [seed]{seed} of the bliss of vajra-lotus union and radiates through the [three worlds]{trailokya}, and in its sky-like nature of [bliss]{sukha} no one is bound or freed (cp.43.m2).

citations.quoted: The world is pervaded by bliss in the form of pervaded and pervader.
citations.work: Hevajra Tantra (cited by Munidatta as the Dvikalpa)

flags.note: vidvān. The print has na ko vidvān mukto vā, 'no one is learned or freed', which is not a pair. Line 1b asks who is bound (bāṇata), the Tibetan line has bcings nas grol ba, and the Tibetan comment has bcings pa dang grol ba med pa, 'there is neither bound nor freed'. vidvān looks like a corruption of baddho (written vaddho), 'bound'. I translate 'bound'; the translit keeps vidvān.

Refrain. Munidatta counts couplets 2, 3 and 4 as his second, third and fourth verses (cp.43.m3, cp.43.m4, cp.43.m5; the Tibetan agrees: rkang pa gnyis pa, gsum pa, bzhi pa). Elsewhere he leaves the refrain out of his count, so here he is not treating couplet 2 as the refrain. He ends his comment on couplet 1 with padasyottarapadena dhruvapadaṃ boddhavyam (cp.43.m2), 'the refrain is to be understood by the latter part of the verse' (Tibetan: tshig phyi ma'i rkang pas d+h+rU'i rkang par rig par bya'o). In its most natural sense, uttarapada is the second half of the couplet he has just explained, so his refrain is 1b ('who is in bonds?'), or couplet 1, and not couplet 2. Shastri's ধ্রু after 1b, which does not usually follow a first couplet, points the same way. A weaker reading, 'by the verse that follows', would make couplet 2 the refrain, but then he would be counting the refrain, against his practice. The song draft keeps couplet 2 as the refrain, and I have not changed it.

The Tibetan comment differs in detail: bde bar byas pa'i sa bon, 'the seed made blissful', for sukhākārabīja; sems su byed pa, with no word for 'radiated' (sphurita); 'the example equal to the sky' (nam mkha' dang mtshungs pa'i dpe) as a separate phrase; and 'great bliss' (bde ba chen po) for bliss (sukha). I follow the Sanskrit.
sphuritaṃ(taḥ) and sahajacitta[ṃ]: the parenthesis and the square bracket are Shastri's. Either form gives 'has radiated'.

segments.translit:
dvitīyapadena dṛṣṭāntopamāṃ karoti—
jima jaletyādi| yathā bāhyanīrāntarapatanabhedo na jñāyate budhaiḥ| tathā manobodhicittaratnayogīndrasamarasībhūtaṃ gaganeti| prabhāsvare viṣati tatra tasya jñānopalambho na[61ka] syād iti|
tathā cāgamaḥ—
yathā jale jalaṃ nyasta[ṃ] jñānacakraṃ tathā sthitam iti|
segments.translation:
With the second [verse]{pada} he makes an [illustrative simile]{drstantopama}: 'As [water in water]{water-in-water}…' and so on. Just as the wise do not know the difference when outer water falls into water, so [the mind, the jewel of bodhicitta]{citta-ratna} has become of the [same taste]{samarasa} as the [lord of yogis]{yogindra}. 'The [sky]{gagana}': it enters [clear light]{prabhasvara}, and there it would have no [apprehension]{upalambha} of [knowledge]{jnana}.
And so the [scripture]{agama}:
'As water placed in water, so the [wheel of knowledge]{jnanacakra} abides.'
segments.note: Munidatta calls this couplet, his second verse, an [illustrative simile]{drstantopama}: as water fallen into water cannot be told apart, so [the mind, the jewel of bodhicitta]{citta-ratna} becomes of the [same taste]{samarasa} as the [lord of yogis]{yogindra} and enters 'the sky', [clear light]{prabhasvara}, with no [apprehension]{upalambha} of knowledge (cp.43.m3). A quoted scripture says the [wheel of knowledge]{jnanacakra} abides so.

citations.quoted: As water placed in water, so the wheel of knowledge abides.

flags.note: Song 2b. Shastri prints maraṇa aaṇā. Munidatta's paraphrase (cp.43.m3) has manobodhicittaratna, 'the mind, the jewel of bodhicitta', and the Tibetan line has yid kyi rin chen, 'jewel of mind' (its comment: yid nyid byang chub kyi sems rin po che). Both support maṇa raaṇā, 'mind-jewel', as in the draft, over maraṇa, 'death'. He quotes only jima jale, so the support comes from his paraphrase, not from a quotation of 2b.
Munidatta introduces this couplet as his second verse (dvitīyapadena, cp.43.m3), not as the refrain. See the refrain flag on cp.43.m2.
viṣati stands for viśati, 'enters' (ṣ for ś). The Tibetan has rab tu zhugs pa, 'entered'.

The Tibetan comment states the example positively: the intelligent know water placed in outer water to be without difference (dbyer med par blo dang ldan pas shes so), where the Sanskrit says the wise do not know the difference. It has 'placed' (bzhag) where the Sanskrit has 'falling' (patana), and it joins the mind-jewel and the lord of yogis with 'and' (dang).

tasya jñānopalambhaḥ, 'apprehension of knowledge', can mean knowledge taken as an object or knowledge grasping an object; the Tibetan (de'i ye shes dmigs pa) is just as open. I keep the literal phrase.

segments.translit:
tṛtīyapadena bhāvasvarūpam āha—
jāsu ṇāhītyādi| yasya yogīndrasya ātmātmīyasambandho na syāt (śyat) tasya parasambandhaḥ sa (sva) itaratara eva| yasmāda(do)nutpannā ye bhāvāḥ teṣām utpādasthitibhaṅgā na dṛśyante(te) siddhapuruṣaiḥ|
tathā cāgamaḥ—
na jāto na mṛ(tva)taś caiva na rūpī nādhirūpavān|
na saṃsāre na nirvāṇe nakāras tena sū(śū)cyate||
segments.translation:
With the third [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of things: 'One who has no…' and so on. The [lord of yogis]{yogindra} who has no relation to [self]{atman} and what belongs to self: for him the relation to others is more remote still. For the things that are [unarisen]{anutpada}, their [arising, abiding and perishing]{utpada-bhanga} are not seen by [siddhas]{siddha}.
And so the [scripture]{agama}:
'Not born and not dead,
neither with [form]{rupa} nor formless,
not in [saṃsāra]{samsara}, not in [nirvāṇa]{nirvana}:
so it is indicated by "not".'
segments.note: Munidatta reads couplet 3, his third verse, as the [true nature]{svarupa} of things: for a [lord of yogis]{yogindra} with no relation to [self]{atman} and what is his own, relation to others is remote, and [siddhas]{siddha} see no arising, abiding or perishing in what has not arisen (cp.43.m4). He quotes a scripture: it is indicated by 'not'.

citations.quoted: Not born and not dead, neither with form nor formless, not in saṃsāra, not in nirvāṇa: so it is indicated by "not".

flags.note: Song 3a. Munidatta quotes only the opening (cp.43.m4), as jāsuṇāhi against the print's jatpuṇāhi, which supports jāsu ṇāhi, 'for whom there is not'. His paraphrase, 'the lord of yogis who has no relation to self and what belongs to self: for him the relation to others is …', supports the relative frame (yasya … tasya), the absence of self, and 'others' (para) as what is at issue, so the draft's 'One who has no self: for him … others' has a basis. It does not support the rest. He does not quote adhyātā sbaparelā kāhi; he speaks of relations (sambandha), not of self and others as such; and he makes a statement (the relation to others is remote), not a question. 'Where are others?' rests on taking kāhi as 'where'. The Tibetan line (gang la gang la bdag nyid med pa de la gzhan dag dang) agrees on 'for whom there is no self, for him others', but it has no question either: it runs on into 3b.

sa (sva) itaratara eva: itaratara, 'more other', is odd. The Tibetan has shin tu ring du gyur pa, 'has become very far off', which suggests a reading such as sudūratara, 'very far'. I translate 'more remote still', which fits both.
In the verse, nādhirūpavān makes poor sense. The Tibetan gzugs med pa'ang min, 'and not formless', suggests nārūpavān, and I translate 'nor formless'.

The Tibetan comment differs in places. In the paraphrase it has 'grasping at self and mine' (bdag dang bdag gir 'dzin pa) with a causal 'because' (med pa'i phyir), and 'unarisen from the first' (dang por ma skyes pa), which matches the song's āi, 'beginning', where the print has only anutpannā. Perhaps the manuscript's yasmādo hides ādau, 'at first', but that is a guess. In the verse it has 'likewise' (de bzhin nyid, as if tathaiva) for caiva, and 'free of doing' (byed pa dang bral), taking nakāra as na + kāra, where I take it as the letter na.
nakāras tena sūcyate: literally 'by this the letter na is indicated', that is, the verse says what the syllable na stands for. I render it 'so it is indicated by "not"'.
The parenthesized forms (śyat), (sva), (do), (te), (tva) and (śū) are Shastri's alternatives, apparently the manuscript's readings. I translate his main text except where flagged.

segments.translit:
caturthapadena bhāvasvarūpam āha—
bhusuku bhaṇai ityādi| kaṭam iti pūrvoktārthaṃ| bhusukupādo vadati| sakalabhāvānām eṣaḥ svarūpaḥ| etasmin gambhīrasahajānandānubhāvād bhāvābhāvavikalpaparihāreṇa na ko 'pi yogī jinasaṃsārakā(cā)rāgāre yātāyātaṃ dṛśyate|
tathā ca sarahapādaḥ—
gambhīra ai uāṇsa uparaṇo apyāṇa||
sahajānanda caujjaha luṇia saṃveaṇa jāṇa|| 43||
segments.translation:
With the fourth [verse]{pada} he states the [true nature]{svarupa} of things: '[Bhusuku]{p-bhusuku} says…' and so on. '[Told]{kata}' means the meaning stated before. [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} says: this is the true nature of all things. In this, through experiencing [profound]{gambhira} [innate joy]{sahajananda}, by abandoning the [conceptual thought]{vikalpa} of [being and nonbeing]{bhava-abhava}, no [yogi]{yogi} at all is seen [coming and going]{coming-and-going} in the prison of birth and [saṃsāra]{samsara}.
And so [Saraha]{p-saraha}:
'The [profound]{gambhira} cannot be pointed to: neither other nor self.
[Innate joy]{sahajananda} …: know it by [self-awareness]{svasamvedana}.'
segments.note: Munidatta explains kaṭa as 'the meaning stated before' (cp.43.m5): [Bhusukupāda]{p-bhusuku} says this is the true nature of all things, and through experiencing profound [innate joy]{sahajananda}, free of concepts of [being and nonbeing]{bhava-abhava}, no yogi is seen coming and going in the prison of birth and [saṃsāra]{samsara}. He passes over [Rāutu]{p-rautu} and quotes [Saraha]{p-saraha}.

citations.quoted: The profound cannot be pointed to: neither other nor self. Innate joy …: know it by self-awareness.
citations.work: a dohā of Saraha (Munidatta names the poet, not the work)

flags.note: kaṭa. Munidatta glosses kaṭam iti pūrvoktārtham, 'kaṭa means the meaning stated before' (cp.43.m5), and the draft's 'told' follows him. The Tibetan line has ngo mtshar, 'wonder', and the Tibetan comment explains ngo mtshar as what Bhusuku 'said directly' (mngon sum du gsungs pa), as if its Sanskrit had some word other than pūrvokta, perhaps one linked to prakaṭa, 'manifest'. The Tibetan therefore reads the line as 'wonder', not 'told'.

Rāutu. Munidatta passes over rāutu bhaṇai kaṭa and paraphrases only 'Bhusukupāda says' (cp.43.m5). In its place the Tibetan line has rjes smras, 'then said' or 'said after', with no name. Neither witness confirms Rāutu as a second speaker here, though the draft of 4a has one.

jina-. The print's jinasaṃsārakārāgāre ('in the Jina's prison of saṃsāra'?) makes poor sense. The Tibetan has 'khor bar skye ba, 'birth in saṃsāra', which suggests jani, 'birth' (জনি for জিন, with the vowel sign on the wrong letter). I translate 'the prison of birth and saṃsāra'.
kā(cā)rāgāre: Shastri prints kārāgāra, 'prison', with cārāgāra in parenthesis. The Tibetan spyod pa khyim du 'jug pa, 'conduct entering a house', seems to render cāra + āgāra. I follow the print.

The Tibetan builds the sentence differently: the yogi is the one who does not see (rnal 'byor pas ma mthong ba) birth in saṃsāra, entering a house, or coming. It has yongs su bsdus pas, 'by gathering up', where the Sanskrit has parihāreṇa, 'by abandoning', and ngo bo, 'nature', where the Sanskrit has anubhāva.

anubhāvāt can mean 'through the power of' (Buddhist Sanskrit anubhāva) or, read as anubhava, 'through experiencing'. I chose 'experiencing', which is how the glossary takes this passage; 'through the power of profound innate joy' is possible.

Saraha's couplet is corrupt in the print. For gambhīra ai uāṇsa I follow the Tibetan zab mo nyid kyang mtshon du med, 'profundity itself cannot be pointed to'. I read uparaṇo apyāṇa as u para ṇo appāṇa, 'neither other nor self' (Tibetan rang dang gzhan du mi dmigs, 'not apprehended as self or other'). caujjaha luṇia is left as '…'. It may hide cauttha, 'the fourth', or ca ujjhaha, 'and abandon', with ṇia for nija, 'own'; the Tibetan has 'the fruit of innate joy' ('bras bu). saṃveaṇa jāṇa: 'know by self-awareness' (Tibetan rang rig nyid kyis shes).

questions: Refrain (cp.43.m2, cp.43.m3): Munidatta counts couplets 2, 3 and 4 as his second, third and fourth verses. He ends his comment on couplet 1 with padasyottarapadena dhruvapadaṃ boddhavyam, most naturally 'the refrain is to be understood by the latter part of the verse', that is, 1b. Together with Shastri's ধ্রু after 1b, this suggests that for him the refrain of this song is 1b (or couplet 1), not couplet 2. I have left the song draft's refrain on couplet 2 untouched. Do you want the refrain moved, or a note on the song saying that Munidatta's arrangement differs?

cp.43.m2: I translate the print's vidvān as 'bound' (baddho), on the evidence of line 1b and the Tibetan bcings pa dang grol ba med pa. Is that emendation acceptable in the translation, or would you rather print 'learned' and explain in a note?

cp.43.m4: Munidatta's paraphrase supports the frame of the reconstructed 3a ('One who has no self: for him … others') but not the question 'where are others?': he says the relation to others is remote, and the Tibetan line has no question either. Is the question form in the draft acceptable?
cp.43.m5 and line 4a: Munidatta passes over rāutu bhaṇai kaṭa, and the Tibetan line has rjes smras, 'then said', with no name. The draft names Rāutu as a second speaker. Keep that, or flag 4a?
cp.43.m5: the draft's 'told' follows Munidatta's pūrvoktārtha, while the Tibetan reads ngo mtshar, 'wonder', and its comment speaks of what was 'said directly'. Keep 'told'?
cp.43.m5: I read jina- as jani, 'birth' (Tibetan 'khor bar skye ba), which gives 'the prison of birth and saṃsāra'. Do you accept that?
cp.43.m5: in Saraha's couplet I left caujjaha luṇia as '…' rather than guess. Would you prefer a conjecture ('the fourth' for cauttha, 'own' for ṇia/nija), or the Tibetan's 'the fruit of innate joy'?
cp.43.m2: Munidatta names the Hevajra as the Dvikalpa, so I used 'Dvikalpa' as the surface for tx-hevajra (a keep-source entry). Would you prefer 'Hevajra'?
